Keywords: btree index, gin index, index type, jsonb index
Guidance: Using the default B-tree index on a JSONB or full-text column gives no meaningful speedup for containment/text queries; GIN indexes are built for exactly that access pattern.
Do: Use GIN indexes for JSONB containment (@>) and full-text search columns; keep B-tree for equality/range on scalar columns.
Don't: Create a B-tree index on a JSONB column and expect it to speed up @> containment queries.
Example: CREATE INDEX idx_data_gin ON events USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops);

Keywords: explain analyze, query plan, seq scan, index scan
Guidance: A Seq Scan on a large table where an index exists is a strong signal the planner's cost estimates or table statistics are off, or the index just isn't usable for that predicate.
Do: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on slow queries and check for unexpected Seq Scans, high loops counts, and row estimate mismatches.
Don't: Tune query performance based on guesses instead of reading the actual query plan.
Example: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

Guidance: Default autovacuum thresholds are tuned for small tables; on large, high-churn tables they run too infrequently, letting dead tuple bloat degrade query performance and risk transaction ID wraparound.
Do: Tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor/threshold per large high-churn table, and monitor n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum.
Don't: Leave default autovacuum settings unchanged on large, high-write tables and never check dead tuple counts.

Keywords: pgbouncer, connection pooling, max_connections, transaction pooling
Guidance: Postgres connections are relatively expensive (each is a full backend process); an app that opens a new connection per request instead of pooling exhausts max_connections under moderate load.
Do: Put PgBouncer (or a client-side pool) in front of Postgres in transaction pooling mode for high-connection-churn workloads.
Don't: Let every application instance open unpooled direct connections to Postgres at scale.

Keywords: replication lag, streaming replication, wal, replica delay
Guidance: Long-running queries or large transactions on the primary generate WAL faster than a replica (especially over a slow network link) can apply it, causing read replicas to serve increasingly stale data.
Do: Monitor pg_stat_replication lag and replica apply rate; watch for large batch writes or vacuum operations on the primary as common lag triggers.
Don't: Assume read replicas are always current with no lag monitoring in place.

Guidance: With no statement_timeout, a single runaway query can hold locks and consume resources indefinitely, and an idle-in-transaction client can block vacuum and other queries for hours.
Do: Set statement_timeout, lock_timeout, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout at the role or database level as a safety net.
Don't: Run production workloads with no statement or idle-transaction timeout configured.

Keywords: n+1 query, orm, batch query, eager loading
Guidance: An ORM lazily fetching related rows one query per parent row (classic N+1) is invisible in local testing with small data but devastates latency at production scale.
Do: Use eager loading / JOINs / batched IN queries for known access patterns instead of per-row lazy fetches.
Don't: Iterate over a result set and issue a separate query per row for related data.
Example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ANY($1::int[]);

Keywords: table partitioning, declarative partitioning, range partition
Guidance: A single unpartitioned table growing past tens/hundreds of millions of rows makes vacuum, index maintenance, and even simple queries progressively slower with no way to prune old data cheaply.
Do: Use declarative range or list partitioning (e.g. by month) for large, time-series-like tables, so old partitions can be dropped instantly.
Don't: Let a high-volume time-series table grow unpartitioned indefinitely.
Example: CREATE TABLE events (ts timestamptz, ...) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts);

Keywords: unused index, duplicate index, index bloat, write amplification
Guidance: Every index adds write overhead on insert/update/delete; unused or duplicate indexes (found via pg_stat_user_indexes) slow writes for zero read benefit.
Do: Periodically audit pg_stat_user_indexes for near-zero idx_scan counts and drop genuinely unused indexes.
Don't: Add indexes speculatively and never revisit whether they're actually used by the query planner.
Example: SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan < 10;

Keywords: foreign key, check constraint, not valid, data integrity
Guidance: Adding a foreign key or check constraint on a large existing table with the default validation locks the table for the duration of the full-table scan.
Do: Add the constraint NOT VALID first (fast), then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately (doesn't block writes) to avoid a long exclusive lock.
Don't: Add a constraint to a large production table with default full validation during business hours.
Example: ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id) NOT VALID;\nALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fk_customer;

Keywords: pitr, wal archiving, base backup, continuous archiving
Guidance: Relying on nightly pg_dump alone means any data loss between the last dump and the incident is unrecoverable; WAL archiving enables recovery to any point in time.
Do: Configure continuous WAL archiving and periodic base backups (or use a managed service's PITR feature) for production databases.
Don't: Rely solely on periodic pg_dump snapshots with no WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery.

Guidance: Without pg_stat_statements enabled, there's no aggregate view of which queries actually consume the most total time in production -- only anecdotal slow-query reports.
Do: Enable pg_stat_statements and periodically review top queries by total_exec_time, not just individual slow-query logs.
Don't: Diagnose database performance issues with no aggregate query statistics extension enabled.
Example: CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements;\nSELECT query, total_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

Keywords: isolation level, serializable, mvcc, serialization failure
Guidance: Using SERIALIZABLE isolation for correctness under concurrent writes means the application must be prepared to retry transactions that fail with a serialization error -- it's not a 'set and forget' setting.
Do: Choose the isolation level deliberately per transaction's correctness needs, and implement retry logic for SERIALIZABLE serialization failures.
Don't: Set SERIALIZABLE isolation without implementing any retry logic for the resulting serialization failures.
Example: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;\n-- retry on SQLSTATE 40001
